items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-05-26
items.q: Well Stein was in the band. So was Nunes at that time.

ctx.x: Can you give the instruments to the people who want to know?

He played clarinet. Eddie Rowland, after two weeks, they were thrown out of a job. And he was put in jail for no visible means of support. There was only one person he knew. And that was me. Because I happened to be the oldest musician of the bunch that ever went off and played up around out of town. And I had to pay his way out of jail was $25. Put him on a train and sent him back to New Orleans. I have never received one penny from him. He's dead now up to this day. Went in a lock, split business, some way down…
What was his name again? Carter?

items.q: Yes, it consisted of three pieces, colon, Nunes, comma, Rags, and Stein, period.

ctx.x: This is a letter. Headed Paris, December 16, 1956. Dear Mr. LaRocca, The very long trip I have done through the world is at its end. I am just arrived from Melbourne this morning with a great regret not to have been in New Orleans for meeting you. But fate is blind and can offer me a very next opportunity to go to the States for another film. I suppose you have well received my letter dated November the 11th that I have sent you from Calcutta. If you don't, I will mail you a copy. The 1956 Olympic Games were very…

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1959-06-14
items.q: That takes Nunes. That takes them all in. None of them could play the rhythm. The only time they ever played that rhythm was when I was there hitting, beating down on them and carrying them.

ctx.x: And they're saying there was some part of the creation of jazz. That Jack Lane, who played a drum and lousy drums at that, created jazz. Now that's good enough for men who thrive on thievery, on a word that we had nothing to do. Our jazz was started in Chicago. We took in the ragtime and changed the rhythm in Chicago. In 1916, we seen we were going to be a flop the first night. And I, being a good dancer, I watched those people. At that time, they had Vernon Castle doing the castle walk. And everybody was trying…

No, I wrote that mostly as a sort of, you might say, editor. Walter Allen managed to interview the various musicians that were still living. And he sent me the facts and I wrote them, sewed them up together. I was more concerned with the records than with the legends. I wasn't very interested in these obscure people from the shadows who were said to have played with this, that and the other musician, in this, that and the other band, and who never made any records at all. I'm not interested in music I can't hear…
